# RedGem 3D Engine

> The manual of RedGem, a 3D game engine where games are written in Ruby.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/

# RedGem 3D Engine

RedGem is a 3D game engine with its own editor. You build levels in the editor (or in Blender),
write the gameplay in **Ruby**, press Play, and export a standalone game.

This manual is for people making games with it.

## Where to start

1. [Install](install.md) the editor.
2. Follow [Your first game](first-game.md): about fifteen minutes from an empty folder to a
   playable game.
3. Keep [Behaviours](scripting/behaviours.md) and the [API reference](scripting/api.md) open while
   you write scripts.
4. [The command line](command-line.md) reads and changes scenes as text, plays a game with no
   window, takes pictures of it and looks it over: handy in scripts and with coding assistants
   (see [Making games with an AI assistant](assistants.md)).

## How a game is organized

A game is a folder:

| Path | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `scene.glb` | The main level: objects, meshes, lights, cameras |
| `scenes/*.glb` | More levels |
| `scripts/*.rb` | Ruby behaviours and scene scripts |
| `models/*.glb` | Models you can drop into a level |
| `prefabs/*.glb` | [Reusable object files](prefabs.md), loaded through scene references |
| `sounds/` | `.wav`, `.ogg`, `.mp3` or `.flac` files |
| `images/` | Pictures for menus and the HUD (`.png`, `.jpg`) |
| `locales/` | The texts players read, one translation file per language: `en.json`, `pt.json`... (see [Texts in several languages](scripting/i18n.md)) |
| `game.json` | The game's id, title and window size |

The editor reads and writes these files directly. There is no project database and no import
step: what you see in the folder is the game.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/install/

# Install

RedGem is experimental. The editor is developed on Linux; there are Windows and macOS downloads
too.
Pick one of the ways below.

## Download (easiest)

| System | Download |
|--------|----------|
| Linux (x86_64) | [redgem-linux-x86_64.tar.gz](https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem/releases/latest/download/redgem-linux-x86_64.tar.gz) |
| Windows (x86_64) | [redgem-windows-x86_64.zip](https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem/releases/latest/download/redgem-windows-x86_64.zip) |
| macOS (Apple Silicon) | [redgem-macos-arm64.zip](https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem/releases/latest/download/redgem-macos-arm64.zip) |
| macOS (Intel) | [redgem-macos-x86_64.zip](https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem/releases/latest/download/redgem-macos-x86_64.zip) |

Unpack it anywhere and run `bin/redgem` (Linux), `redgem.exe` (Windows) or open `RedGem.app`
(macOS). Nothing is installed: delete the folder to remove it. The demos are in its `games/` folder.

- **Linux** needs a desktop with OpenGL 3.3, a processor with AVX2 and glibc 2.39 or newer
  (Ubuntu 24.04 and later). It builds games for Linux, Windows and Android.
- **Windows** is compiled from Linux and has only been tried under Wine, not on a real Windows
  machine yet. It builds games for Windows.
- **macOS** needs macOS 11 or newer. It is built and tested on GitHub's Mac machines (macOS 14 on
  Apple Silicon, macOS 15 on Intel), which are virtual machines with no graphics card OpenGL can
  use: there the editor opens, edits, plays and saves a game drawn by Apple's software renderer.
  It has not been tried on a real Mac yet. It builds games for the Mac only.
  The app is not signed by a registered Apple developer nor notarized, so macOS refuses it the
  first time: right-click `RedGem.app` and choose *Open* (on macOS 15 and later: try once, then
  *System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway*), or run
  `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine RedGem.app` in the unpacked folder.

Wherever this manual says `./build/src/redgem ...`, write `bin/redgem ...` (or `redgem.exe ...`,
or `RedGem.app/Contents/MacOS/redgem ...` on macOS).

## With Docker

You need [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) and a desktop session using X11.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem.git
cd redgem
tools/docker/editor.sh
```

The first run builds the image, which takes a few minutes. After that the editor opens in seconds.

- Games you create are saved in `~/RedGemGames` on your machine.
- The demos are in the `games/` folder of the checkout: `tools/docker/editor.sh games/platformer`.
- The script takes the same arguments as `redgem` itself, so wherever this manual says
  `./build/src/redgem ...`, write `tools/docker/editor.sh ...`. Paths must be inside
  `~/RedGemGames` or the checkout's `games/` folder: the container sees nothing else.
- The container has no sound.

## From source

You need a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.24 or newer, Ninja, Ruby with rake, and the X11 and OpenGL
development files. On Ubuntu or Debian:

```bash
sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build git ca-certificates xz-utils ruby rake bison \
  libgl1-mesa-dev libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libasound2-dev
```

On macOS: the Xcode command line tools (`xcode-select --install`), then
`brew install cmake ninja` and a Ruby with rake (the CI builds with Ruby 3.3).

Then:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
./build/src/redgem
```

CMake downloads the libraries RedGem is built on at fixed versions. The first build takes a few
minutes.

## Check that it works

`./build/src/redgem` (or `tools/docker/editor.sh`) opens the **project hub**. Choose
*Platformer* under *New game*, give it a name, and the editor opens with a level you can play
right away: press the Play button, move with WASD, jump with Space.

`./build/src/redgem --version` says which version you have (`RedGem 0.5.0`, say): give it when
you report a problem. (`redgem --help` lists everything else the command line does.)

## Blender (optional)

You can make whole games without it. Install [Blender](https://www.blender.org) 4.x when you want
to model your own objects or build levels there: see [Levels, lighting and Blender](levels.md).

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/first-game/

# Your first game

You will create a game from a template, change it, write a behaviour in Ruby and export it.

## 1. Create the game

Start RedGem with no arguments. In the project hub, pick the **Platformer** template, type a name
and create it. The same from a terminal:

```bash
./build/src/redgem new ~/RedGemGames/my_game --template platformer
./build/src/redgem ~/RedGemGames/my_game
```

With Docker, write `tools/docker/editor.sh` wherever this manual says `./build/src/redgem`.

The editor opens:

- **Scene** (center): the level. Hold the right mouse button and use WASD to fly, scroll to move
  closer, click an object to select it.
- **Hierarchy** (left): every object of the level.
- **Inspector** (right): what the selected object is made of.
- **Project** and **Console** (bottom): the game's files, and messages from the engine and from
  your scripts.

## 2. Play it

Press **Play** in the toolbar (or Ctrl+P). The game runs inside the Scene view: WASD moves, Space
jumps. Press Esc or **Stop** to go back to editing. The level returns exactly to how it was.

## 3. Change the level

1. Click a coin in the Scene view.
2. Drag the arrows of the gizmo to move it somewhere harder to reach.
3. Press Ctrl+D to duplicate it and move the copy too.
4. Press Ctrl+S to save.

Ctrl+Z undoes any of this.

## 4. Write a behaviour

Make the hero's coins worth collecting: a platform that moves up and down.

1. In the menu, **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**. Scale and place it as a platform.
2. In the Inspector, **Add Component > Script**, type `bob` and press **New**.
3. The script opens in a tab next to the Scene. Replace its contents with:

```ruby
# Moves the object up and down.
class Bob < Behaviour
  HEIGHT = 2.0   # meters
  SECONDS = 4.0  # per cycle

  def start
    @origin = transform.position
  end

  def update(_dt)
    wave = Math.sin(Time.elapsed / SECONDS * 2 * Math::PI)
    transform.position = @origin + Vector3.up * (wave * HEIGHT)
  end
end
```

4. Press Ctrl+S. The tab shows *Syntax OK*, or the line of the mistake.
5. With the cube selected, find the **Physics** card in the Inspector and set *Body* to
   *kinematic*, so the hero can stand on it while it moves.
6. Press Play.

If a script fails while the game runs, the game keeps going: that behaviour is switched off and
the error, with its line, appears in the Console.

## 5. Share it

**Build** in the toolbar (or `redgem build <game> <folder>`) makes a folder with your game's
executable and its files, for Linux, Windows or (from a Mac) macOS. Zip it and send it. See [Building and sharing](shipping.md).

## Next

- [Behaviours](scripting/behaviours.md): how scripts are attached and what they can do.
- [Gameplay recipes](scripting/gameplay.md): input, movement, pickups, HUD, sound, levels.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/editor/

# The editor

```bash
./build/src/redgem games/platformer          # opens the editor
./build/src/redgem games/platformer --play   # just plays the game
```

The editor is built with Dear ImGui (dark theme, Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts, Font Awesome
icons):

* **Toolbar**: move / rotate / scale gizmos, local or world axes, the pivot several selected objects
  turn and scale around (their middle, or the first one selected), grid snapping (or hold Ctrl
  while dragging), Play / Pause / Stop, and Build.
* **Hierarchy**: the object tree with search. Click to select, Ctrl+click to add an object to the
  selection or take it away, Shift+click to select every row from the last one clicked; double
  click to frame, drag onto another object to parent it (or onto empty space to unparent; a row of
  the selection takes the whole selection along), right click for actions (on the whole selection) and to create objects. Scripts and models from the
  Project panel can be dropped on it.
* **Scene**: hold the right mouse button and use WASD/QE to fly, wheel to dolly, F to frame the
  selection, click to pick objects (Ctrl or Shift + click adds or takes away), drag a rectangle to
  select what shows inside it (with Ctrl or Shift held, added to the selection), W / E / R switch
  the gizmo. Drop a model on the ground to place it there, or a script on an object to attach it.
* **Inspector**: name, tag, visible, *Template* (hidden in the game, copied with `Scene.spawn`), then
  one card per component: Transform, Mesh with its materials (color, metallic, roughness, emission
  and their pictures, see [Material pictures](#material-pictures)),
  Light (type, color, intensity, range), Camera (field of view, clipping), one card per Ruby script,
  Physics (body, trigger, collider, mass), vehicle wheels and custom properties. **Add Component**
  adds scripts (existing or new), a physics body, a trigger or a property. With several objects
  selected it shows what they have in common: tag, visible, *Template* and the Transform, a dash
  where their values differ. An edit applies to all of them.
* **GameObject menu**: terrain you sculpt with a brush (see [Levels](levels.md#terrain)), empty
  objects, cube / sphere / plane / cylinder / capsule (with colliders),
  directional / point / spot lights, cameras, and the game's models.
* **Your own models, sounds and pictures**: drop `.glb` files (exported from Blender), `.wav` /
  `.ogg` / `.mp3` / `.flac` files and `.png` / `.jpg` / `.jpeg` / `.webp` pictures from your file
  manager onto the editor window. They are copied into the game's `models/`, `sounds/` and
  `images/` folders and show up in the Project panel.
* **Project**: the game's scripts, models, sounds, scenes and images. Double click a script to edit
  it, a model to add it to the scene, a sound to hear it, a scene to open it (see [Scenes](#scenes)),
  a picture to see it in your system's viewer.
  *New script* creates a `Behaviour` from a template, *New scene* a scene; *Open folder* shows the
  files.
* **Console**: engine and Ruby output (filter by level), including script errors with backtraces.
* **Scripts**: each open Ruby file gets its own tab next to the Scene. Drag tabs to split the view
  anywhere (or press *Split right*), like a code editor's editor groups. The code is colored as
  you type: keywords, strings, symbols, comments, numbers, constants and `@variables` each have a
  color of the editor's theme. Ctrl+S saves and checks
  the syntax (errors show the line); *Open externally* uses your default editor. Play saves all
  open scripts and reloads them.
* **Agent**: a chat with a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex or one of your own), in a tab beside
  the Inspector. It works in the game's folder and sees and changes the open scene through the
  editor's tools; see [The Agent panel](assistants.md#the-agent-panel).
* **View menu**: hide the Hierarchy (Ctrl+B), the Inspector (Ctrl+Alt+B) or the bottom panels
  (Ctrl+J) to give the scene or the code more room; the toolbar's outer buttons toggle the sides.
* **Play / Pause / Stop** (Ctrl+P, Esc): runs the game inside the Scene view with the current edits
  and fresh scripts; Stop restores the scene exactly as it was.
* **Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y** undo and redo, **Ctrl+D** duplicate, **Del** delete, **Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C /
  Ctrl+V** cut, copy and paste, **Ctrl+S** save. Help > Keyboard Shortcuts lists them all. File >
  New / Open Game goes back to the hub.

## Material pictures

Under a material's color, metallic, roughness and emission, the Inspector lists its five texture
slots, each with the picture it shows or *None*:

* **Color map**: the surface's colors, tinted by the material's color.
* **Surface map**: roughness in the green channel and metalness in the blue one (glTF's
  metallic-roughness map), scaled by the sliders.
* **Normal map**: small bumps and grooves, as a tangent-space normal map.
* **Occlusion map**: how much ambient light reaches each spot, in the red channel.
* **Glow map**: where the surface glows, tinted by the emission color.

Click a slot to pick one of the pictures of the game's `images/` folder (or *None*), or drag a
picture from the Project panel's Images onto it. The picture goes inside the scene's `.glb` (the
same picture used twice is stored once), so the scene still shows it in Blender and when copied to
another scene; a picture no material shows any more is left out when the scene is saved. Each
change is one undo step. PNG, JPEG and still WebP pictures can be used.

## Several objects at once

Everything selected moves, turns and scales together with the gizmo (around the middle of the
selection, or around the first object selected: the toolbar's pivot button; a scale goes along the
pivot's axes, and an object turned another way and stretched unevenly takes the nearest placement
without shear), and Duplicate, Delete,
Cut, Copy and Paste act on all of it. A child goes along with its selected parent. Each of these is
one undo step, however many objects it touches.

**Copy** takes the selected objects with everything under them: their meshes, materials, pictures,
skeletons and animations, scripts and properties, lights and cameras. **Paste** (Ctrl+V) puts them
next to the selected object, or at the top level when nothing is selected; **Paste as Child**
(Ctrl+Shift+V, or the Hierarchy's menu) puts them under the selected object. They land where they
were in the world, and a name that is already taken gets a number (`Crate.001`). Paste works in the
scene they came from, in another scene of the game (open it and paste), and in another editor
window: the copy goes on the system's clipboard as text. A copy bigger than 64 MB stays in the
editor's own clipboard and pastes only in the window it was copied in.

A pasted object has its own copy of its meshes and pictures, even in the scene it was copied from
(Duplicate shares them instead).

Undo goes back up to 200 steps, and keeps at most 256 MB for them (its copies of the objects and
terrains, and what deleted objects and undone imports were made of: vertices, pictures and their
bytes in the scene's file; an estimate, counted as each step begins): past either, the oldest steps
go, and what no step can bring back any more is let go of, so a long session with many imports does
not keep growing. The latest step always stays, however big.

Saving rewrites the open scene's file in place (only the glTF JSON; meshes and textures are
untouched), so the file still opens in Blender. When the file changes on disk (e.g. you re-export
from Blender) the editor reloads it automatically, unless you have unsaved edits.

## Scenes

A game can have several scenes: levels, missions, menus. Each is a `.glb` file, known by the name
a script loads it with:

| Scene | File | Loaded with |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `main` | `scene.glb` | `Game.load_scene("main")` |
| `level2` | `scenes/level2.glb` | `Game.load_scene("level2")` |

The game always starts on `main` (`scene.glb`); scripts move to the others with
`Game.load_scene`. The editor opens on `main` too, and edits one scene at a time:

* **Open** another scene with a double click in the Project panel's *Scenes* folder, or with
  File > Open Scene. When the open scene has unsaved edits, the editor asks first (Save, Discard
  or Cancel), like when closing. Each scene has its own undo history: it starts empty when the
  scene opens.
* **New scene** (File > New Scene, or *New scene* in the *Scenes* folder) makes
  `scenes/<name>.glb` with ground, a sun and a camera, and opens it. Names are lowercase letters,
  digits, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter (`level2`, `boss-fight`); `main` is taken.
* **Save** (Ctrl+S) writes the open scene back to its own file. File > Save Scene As writes it as a
  new scene of the game, which is then the one open. A scene that uses files next to it (textures
  exported outside the `.glb`) is not saved into another folder that way, where it would not find
  them: export it from Blender as a `.glb` with its textures in it first.
* **Play** starts the game on the open scene as it is edited, under its own name
  (`Game.scene_name`, and its `scripts/<name>_scene.rb` runs). Stop comes back to it.

The window title and the status bar name the open scene, and the editor follows that scene's file
for changes made outside. Built games carry every scene: Build copies the whole game folder,
`scenes/` included.

## Building

**Build** (in the toolbar, or File > Build Game) asks which system to build for, saves the open
scene and the scripts, and builds the game into a folder beside it: `<game>-build` for the system
the editor runs on, `<game>-build-<system>` for another one (see
[Building and sharing](shipping.md)). The build
runs in the background, so the editor keeps working while it does: a box in the Scene view's
bottom-right corner shows what is being built, for how long it has been, and the step it is at
(copying the game's files, packing the app, signing it). When it ends, the box says how it went:
the folder it filled, with **Open folder**, or what went wrong. The Console keeps the same lines.

One build runs at a time: Build is greyed out until the running one ends. The build reads the
game's files from disk, never the scene open in the editor, so you can keep editing while it runs;
what you save meanwhile is only sure to be in the next build. Closing the editor while a build
runs waits for it, saying so, then closes as usual, asking first about anything edited and not
saved (**Keep the editor open** stays instead).
A build is not stopped halfway: the tools it runs would leave half-written files behind.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/prefabs/

# Prefab files

A scene can refer to a reusable object stored in `prefabs/crate.glb` inside the game
folder. Keep exactly one root in that file. On an empty scene object, set the string
custom property `prefab_file` to `prefabs/crate.glb`. Paths are relative to the game
folder, including references inside another prefab. Symbolic links and paths outside
the game are refused.

Loading replaces the empty object's content with the prefab root's content. The
placement keeps its name, identity and parent. Its transform combines with the
source root's transform. Its custom properties override the source root's properties;
its existing children remain. Descendants come from the file. Geometry, materials
and images are shared by repeated instances of the same file.

A source root marked `prefab = true` becomes live when placed. Mark the reference
itself `prefab = true` to keep an inert template for `Scene.spawn` instead. Each scene
load reads the current files; changing a prefab does not update a running scene.

Descendant identities are deterministic for the source file path, placement identity
and source node identity. Renaming a source node preserves an explicit identity;
renaming the prefab file changes the generated descendant identities. Root placement
identities remain unchanged.

Animate descendants rather than the source root. Imported clips are named
`prefabs/crate.glb::Idle`, for example. Repeated instances share that clip's name;
per-object animation playback still affects only that object's hierarchy. Animated
placements require an identity transform on the source root.

Cycles and oversized expansions fail the load before replacing the running scene.
Defaults allow 64 source files, eight nested references, 4,096 instances and 100,000
expanded nodes, with 256 MiB of source GLB files and 512 MiB of estimated expanded
content. The GLB reader also checks a tighter memory budget before reading buffers.

This first implementation supports runtime loading, editor Play and project checks.
The editing viewport still shows the authored reference node. Creating prefab files,
placing them through the editor and previewing inherited children are separate editor
work; save the source file through your modeling tool for now. Built games include
regular files in `prefabs/` along with the other game assets.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/levels/

# Levels, lighting and Blender

## How a scene is made

1. Model the level in Blender. Gameplay is configured with **custom properties**
   (*Object Properties → Custom Properties*), e.g. `script = "coin.rb"`, `trigger = true`.
2. Export to `scene.glb` (glTF binary). The exporter writes custom properties to each node's `extras`.
3. The runtime loads the `.glb` with cgltf, reads the extras, builds physics bodies and instantiates
   the Ruby class named after each script (`camera_follow.rb` → `CameraFollow`).

A game is just a folder:

```
games/platformer/
  scene.glb          # exported from Blender
  platformer.blend   # the editable source
  scripts/*.rb       # behaviours
```

## Look of a scene: environment, lights and effects

Scenes are drawn in HDR and finished with bloom (bright things glow), filmic tone mapping, a
vignette and anti-aliasing. One object with the property `environment = true` (GameObject >
Environment in the editor, or a Blender empty) sets the mood through its properties:

| Property | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `sky_top`, `sky_horizon`, `ground_color` | colors of the sky gradient, as `#rrggbb`; they also light the scene |
| `fog_color`, `fog_density` | distance fog (it follows the horizon color unless given its own) |
| `ambient`, `exposure` | strength of the sky's light, overall brightness |
| `bloom`, `vignette`, `sun_glow` | glow around bright things, dark corners, the sun's disc and halo (0 turns each off) |
| `wind` | how much foliage sways |
| `shadows` | darkness of the sun's shadows (0 = none, 1 = full) |
| `ambient_occlusion` | darkening of creases and contact areas (0 = none, 1 = full) |
| `contrast`, `saturation` | the finished picture's grade: 1 leaves it as it is |
| `grain`, `aberration` | film grain, and color fringes toward the corners as through a lens (0 turns each off) |
| `sky_image`, `sky_rotation`, `sky_intensity` | a picture of the sky in the game's `images/` folder, drawn behind everything and lighting the scene (see "A sky picture"), the degrees it is turned around the vertical, and its brightness (1 = as the picture is) |
| `msaa` | samples per pixel of the scene's picture (2, 4 or 8; 0, the default, is one): smoother edges, and grass and leaves whose cut-out edges are smoothed too |
| `antialias` | `"temporal"` smooths edges with the frames before (see "Large outdoor scenes"); anything else, the default, smooths them after the picture is drawn |
| `shadow_cascades`, `shadow_distance` | sun shadows over a large area: 1 to 4 maps, each farther from the camera, reaching `shadow_distance` meters (150 unless given) |
| `shadow_softness` | how wide the sun is, in degrees: shadows grow softer the farther they fall from what casts them (the real sun is about 0.5; 0, the default, keeps every edge equally soft) |
| `glow_limit` | the brightest glowing particles together make a pixel, in linear light (2 to 4 suits fire): many flames or sparks over each other come near it and keep their color instead of washing out to white (0, the default, sets no limit) |

Without one, scenes get a clear day. Other things worth knowing: the 16 point lights nearest to the
camera are used each frame (so a street can have dozens of lamps); the sun casts soft shadows
around the camera; and materials use their glTF normal, roughness/metallic, occlusion and emission
textures. A light's intensity and color can change while the game runs (see
[Gameplay recipes](scripting/gameplay.md#light-that-flickers-and-fades)).

### See-through materials and wind

Blender's material settings decide how a material shows what is behind it (the glTF exporter
writes them as the material's alpha mode):

| Alpha mode | Drawn as | For |
|------------|----------|-----|
| Opaque | whole: its alpha is not looked at | almost everything |
| Mask (alpha clip) | cut out where its alpha is below the material's cutoff | leaves, grass, fences |
| Blend | see-through: mixed with what is behind it by its alpha | glass, hair cards, fur, smoke on a card |

A blended material is drawn in two steps. What of it is nearly opaque (alpha 0.9 and above) is
drawn with the opaque surfaces, so that a dozen hair cards over each other still sort themselves
out; the rest is drawn after every opaque surface, mixed with what is behind it, one object at a
time from the farthest to the nearest. Two see-through parts of the same object are not sorted
between themselves, nor are copies scattered with `Scatter.place`. For many layers of fine cards
(fur, a mane), give the material the custom property `transparency = "dithered"` (Material
Properties → Custom Properties, exported when the exporter's *Custom Properties* is on): its texels
are then left out in a fine pattern that thins with their alpha, which needs no sorting at all,
at the price of a slight grain.

**Wind.** Textured cut-out and blended materials are foliage: drawn on both sides, and swaying
with the environment's `wind`. An object whose foliage must stay still gives itself `sway =
false`; objects moved by a skeleton (characters, and so their hair) do not sway unless they say
`sway = true`. Copies scattered from an object sway as it does.

Glossy surfaces reflect their surroundings: the engine keeps capturing the scene around the camera
(one cube face per frame) and uses it for reflections and ambient light.

**A sky picture.** `sky_image = "meadow_sky"` puts a picture of the whole sky around the scene
(`images/meadow_sky.hdr`, `.png` or `.jpg`): an *equirectangular* picture, twice as wide as it is
high, the kind sites of free skies offer and Blender takes as a world texture. It is laid as
Blender lays it (the middle of the picture toward +X; `sky_rotation` turns it), and it lights the
scene in place of the gradient: matte surfaces take the light of the sky around them, and glossy
ones reflect it, sharper the smoother they are. Give the picture's sun a sun light of its own
pointing the same way (the picture's own sun is held down in the light it gives, so that it does
not light the scene twice) and set `ambient` to 1 for the sky's light as the picture has it.
A Radiance picture (`.hdr`) holds light brighter than white, as a real sky has; a PNG or JPEG
stops at white, and `sky_intensity` makes up for it. Pictures are read up to 8192 pixels a side;
the sky drawn behind everything is kept at 4096 pixels across, its light is worked out from a
smaller copy when the scene is loaded (a fraction of a second).

**Large outdoor scenes.** With `shadow_cascades = 4` the sun's shadows reach `shadow_distance`
meters, sharp up close and coarser far away; `shadow_softness = 1.5` widens their edges with the
distance to what casts them (a tree's shadow is sharp at its trunk and soft at its crown). Each
cascade draws the scene's casters once more: a forest of tens of thousands of copies costs more
with four than with one. `msaa = 4` smooths edges with four samples a pixel; cut-out materials
(grass, leaves) then let those samples smooth their edges too, which keeps a meadow from
shimmering as the camera moves. Without it, cut-out edges are smoothed afterwards with the rest of
the picture.

`antialias = "temporal"` goes further: each frame the view moves by less than a pixel, a different
amount every frame, and the frames before, followed to where each pixel was then, are mixed into
this one. Thin grass, leaves and the glints of shiny surfaces stop shimmering, and copies fading
out by distance turn from a fine pattern into an even shade. What moves is followed, characters'
bones and swaying foliage included; what is no longer there (a lightning flash, a character
running past, the camera cutting to another place) is not smeared over the picture; particles
take less of the frames before. A new scene, a new window size and a camera that jumps start over.
It works with `msaa` on or off and costs one more pass over the scene's opaque surfaces.
History fades out locally between 16 and 32 pixels of motion per frame, and at large motion
splits around opening edges. Fast scenery therefore favors current detail, while a tracked
subject with little screen motion still accumulates samples. Reprojected previous-frame depth
rejects hidden or newly revealed surfaces, including moving and skinned objects. A still view
holds still and its edges, against the sky or other surfaces, settle smooth: depth is compared
around where each pixel was, so a silhouette keeps its history. Thin cut-outs and very fast details can still
shimmer as fewer temporal samples are retained.

**Animated characters.** glTF skeletons and animations are supported: skinned meshes are deformed on
the GPU (up to 1024 bones per skeleton, 4 per vertex: a character with fingers has about 65) and every animation in the scene plays in a
loop until a script says otherwise (see [Control animations](scripting/gameplay.md#control-animations)). The editor keeps skeletons and animations when saving, reordering or importing models.
`tools/blender/walk_rig.py` gives a scanned standing person leg bones and a walk cycle.

**Per-object color.** The property `tint = "#rrggbb"` multiplies the colors of an object's mesh, so
copies sharing one mesh (cars, crates) can each have their own color.

**No shadow.** `cast_shadow = false` keeps an object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome, a glow,
a light's shade): it is still drawn and still receives shadows.

**Graphics card.** On laptops with two cards the engine asks for the dedicated one and logs which
card it got. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor (saved in
`~/.config/redgem/settings.json`, used from the next start), the `REDGEM_GPU` environment
variable (read by `redgem` and `redgem-test`), or `--gpu auto|dedicated|integrated` for one run. The command line wins over the
environment, which wins over the saved setting.

**Performance.** Objects outside the view, and parts too small to see from where the camera is, are
not drawn. Objects that share a mesh (linked duplicates in Blender, Alt+D, or copies of one model)
and come one after the other in the level are drawn together, every copy of a part in one call,
however many there are: a street of the same building costs little more than one. Blender keeps
duplicates together by their names (Tree, Tree.001, Tree.002...); copies whose turn comes between
other objects are drawn in that order, so that surfaces lying on each other look as they did. What still costs is the number of different meshes on
screen, and of separate parts in each: join the parts of a model that share a material, and give
heavy models lighter versions for far away with `visible_from` and `visible_to`.

### Coated materials

Blender's Principled BSDF coat is read through `KHR_materials_clearcoat`. A polished coating
can sit above rough paint, wood or a textured base. Its weight and roughness have independent
linear maps (red and green channels respectively), and its normal map does not change the base
normal. The coating reflects the sun, point lights and the environment while attenuating the
base layer and emission by Fresnel, rather than adding unlimited brightness.

Export the coat with the material in glTF. A zero coat weight preserves the original shading.
The editor keeps its factors, texture references and normal scale through import and saving.
The layering follows the [glTF clearcoat extension](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_clearcoat).

## Grass, forests and cities

Tens of thousands of copies (a meadow's grass, a forest) are too many to be objects: a script
scatters them instead (`Scatter.place`, see the [API reference](scripting/api.md)). Model one tuft
or one tree, give it `prefab = true` so the template itself is hidden in the game, and scatter it
over the ground from a scene script's `setup`:

```ruby
Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: [Vector3[-80, 0, -80], Vector3[80, 0, 80]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, scale: 0.7..1.4, align: true)
Scatter.place("Tree", count: 2_000, area: [Vector3[-140, 0, -140], Vector3[140, 0, -90]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 8, scale: 0.8..1.5)
```

The copies take the template's own mesh (a model whose parts are children: join them), its scale,
tint, `visible_from` / `visible_to` and `cast_shadow`. They are only drawn: nothing collides with them (give the
trees a collider of their own, or invisible objects, where players must not walk through) and no
script runs on them. The same seed places them the same on every machine of a game.

They are drawn by patches of ground 16 m across: a patch out of view, or too far for its biggest
copy to show, is skipped whole. Like any object, they cast shadows, and small things (grass) only
near the camera: a tuft half a meter high stops casting one about 50 m away, a tree hundreds of
meters away. Their foliage sways in the wind (`wind` on the environment), each copy with its own
phase, so a field does not move in step.

How the copies look can vary too, the same for the same seed on every machine:

```ruby
Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: field, ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, align: true,
              tints: [[0.85, 1.0, 0.7], [1.05, 1.0, 0.8]],  # each a color between these
              tint_variation: 0.12,                         # and a little brighter or darker
              fade: 10.0,                                   # fading out over the last 10 m
              normals_up: 0.7)                              # lit as the meadow, not as flat cards
```

`fade` makes copies near the template's `visible_to` thin out pixel by pixel over that many meters
instead of popping away (and fade in after its `visible_from`, when it has one: two levels of
detail whose distances overlap by the fade cross over without a gap). `normals_up` bends the
copies' normals toward their own up: grass cards are then lit as the ground they stand on, so a
field does not show the cards' faces turning light and dark with the sun.

### Scatter distance LODs

Use lighter templates to keep vegetation visible far away without drawing the full mesh:

```ruby
forest = Scatter.place("Tree", count: 2_000, area: [corner_a, corner_b], seed: 7,
                       fade: 8.0, lods: [["TreeMid", 40.0], ["TreeFar", 120.0]])
```

All levels share the base template's placement, scale, tint, wind and shadow settings. Each
replacement contributes only its mesh and materials; model it with the same origin, orientation
and dimensions. The base template's `visible_from` and `visible_to` bound the whole chain.

At 40 meters the middle mesh begins appearing; over the next 8 meters it replaces the near
mesh through complementary dithered pixels. The far mesh takes over from 120 to 128 meters.
A zero `fade` switches immediately. Up to three replacements are supported. Distances must
increase, leaving more than `fade` meters between transitions and before `visible_to`.

`count` reports placed copies and `remove` removes the whole chain. Each representation uses
one drawing record per copy: this example uses 6,000 of the scene's 262,144-record budget.
An invalid chain or an exhausted budget adds nothing. Omitting `lods` keeps the original rendering.

## Terrain

**GameObject > Terrain** adds a square of ground, 100 m across, that you shape with a brush. It
comes selected with the brush on: mountains, holes and plateaus are a drag of the mouse away.

1. Drag the left mouse button over the ground in the Scene view. A ring shows the brush.
2. In the Inspector's **Terrain** card, pick what the brush does (**Sculpt** turns the brush off
   and on again, to move the terrain itself with the gizmo):

| Brush | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| Raise | Piles ground up under the brush (hold Shift to dig instead) |
| Lower | Digs (hold Shift to pile up) |
| Smooth | Softens bumps and edges |
| Flatten | Levels the ground to the height at the brush's center: plateaus, roads |

*Radius* is the size of the brush in meters, *Strength* how fast it works. Each stroke is one
undo step. Untick Sculpt to select and move objects again.

The terrain's collider follows its shape, so characters walk and things roll on the hills you
make. Its color and roughness are in the Mesh card, like any object's. A terrain is made and
shaped in the editor; one re-exported from Blender is an ordinary mesh.

## Editing the level in Blender

```bash
blender games/platformer/platformer.blend           # edit, save
blender -b games/platformer/platformer.blend \
  --python tools/blender/export_scene.py -- games/platformer/scene.glb
```

`tools/blender/run.sh build_platformer.py games/platformer` (or `build_driving.py games/driving`)
regenerates a whole level from code; `tools/blender/scene_kit.py` has helpers to build levels with `bpy`.

### Custom properties

| Property   | Values                                         | Meaning |
|------------|------------------------------------------------|---------|
| `script`   | `"player.rb"` or `"a.rb, b.rb"`                | Behaviours to attach, loaded from `scripts/` |
| `body`     | `static`, `dynamic`, `kinematic`, `character`, `vehicle` | Physics body (characters use Jolt's `CharacterVirtual`, vehicles its `VehicleConstraint`) |
| `wheel`    | `true`                                         | On a child of a `vehicle`: it becomes a wheel (model it with its axle along X) |
| `collider` | `box`, `sphere`, `capsule`, `mesh`             | Shape, sized from the mesh bounds × object scale. `collider` alone = static body |
| `trigger`  | `true`                                         | Trigger volume: fires `on_trigger_enter/exit`, does not collide |
| `mass`     | number                                         | Mass of dynamic bodies (and of kinematic ones, should a script make them dynamic) |
| `layer`    | a layer of `game.json`, e.g. `"enemy"`         | Collision layer of the body or trigger: what it meets (see "Collision layers" in the gameplay recipes). Without it, `default` |
| `tag`      | string                                         | Used by `Scene.find_all(tag)` and `game_object.tag?` |
| `visible`  | `false`                                        | Hide the mesh (the object still exists) |
| `prefab`   | `true`                                         | A template: hidden and inert in the game, copied by `Scene.spawn` |
| `prefab_file` | `prefabs/crate.glb` | An empty object loads a [reusable object file](prefabs.md) at its placement |
| `visible_from`, `visible_to` | meters                          | The object is drawn only while that far from the camera: give a model a detailed version up close and a light one far away |
| `tint`     | `"#rrggbb"`                                    | Multiplies the colors of this object's mesh (copies sharing a mesh can differ) |
| `cast_shadow` | `false`                                     | Keeps the object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome) |
| `sway`     | `true` / `false`                               | Whether the wind sways its foliage: unless said, yes, except on objects a skeleton moves (see "See-through materials and wind") |
| `environment` | `true`                                      | This object's properties set the sky, fog and effects (see "Look of a scene") |
| anything   | number / string / bool                         | Available in Ruby as `props[:name]` / `prop(:name, default)` |

Cameras and lights (sun, point) are taken from the Blender scene. Spot lights are loaded but lit
like point lights (in every direction). Parenting is preserved.

**Vehicles.** Give the chassis `body = "vehicle"` and parent the wheel meshes to it with `wheel = true`.
Wheels in front of the center (Blender `+Y`) steer, the rear ones get the hand brake, and every axle
is driven. Wheel radius and width come from the wheel mesh. See `tools/blender/build_driving.py`.
Blender is Z-up; the engine is Y-up like glTF: Blender `(x, y, z)` is engine `(x, z, -y)`
(`Vector3.blender(x, y, z)` does the conversion). Forward is `-Z` (Blender `+Y`).


## Water surfaces

A horizontal, upward-facing mesh becomes water when its material has the Blender custom
property `water = true`. Enable custom properties in the glTF export. The surface is drawn
after opaque geometry: it refracts that picture, absorbs light through the depth behind it,
and reflects on-screen objects with a sky and surroundings fallback. The material's base color is its deep-water
color and roughness controls its reflections. Its alpha is ignored; transparency comes from
water depth and absorption instead.

| Material custom property | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `water` | `false` | Use water shading. |
| `wave_height` | `0.08` | Maximum vertical displacement in world meters, from 0 to 10. |
| `wavelength` | `3` | Dominant wavelength in meters, from 0.05 to 1000. |
| `wave_speed` | `1` | Wave clock multiplier, from 0 (still) to 10. |
| `absorption_red` | `0.35` | Red light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. |
| `absorption_green` | `0.08` | Green light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. |
| `absorption_blue` | `0.035` | Blue light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. |
| `foam_width` | `0.12` | Nominal local horizontal width of a shore foam band, in meters; 0 disables it. World-space patches vary its reach from 0.85 to 1.15 times this value. |
| `refraction` | `0.035` | Refraction strength, from 0 to 0.1; the default uses water's IOR of 1.333 and 0 keeps the bottom undistorted. |

The Blender helper `scene_kit.water_material("Pond", wave_height=0.04, wavelength=2.0)`
creates the material and its custom properties. Optional keyword arguments override the table
above. The material preview has water's IOR and transmission; runtime waves and depth-based
color are applied by the engine after export.

Use a subdivided mesh: vertex spacing at most one tenth of the smallest visible geometric
wavelength avoids angular silhouettes. Three traveling waves displace geometry; finer ripples
change normals. Smooth spatial phase variation curves the crests without changing the maximum height.
The pattern is in world coordinates, so adjacent patches share phase and mesh
scale does not change the wavelength. Wave displacement follows the renderer's clock, including
fixed-step recordings, and the temporal coverage pass uses the same displaced geometry.
Water does not cast an opaque shadow. Objects keep their authored collision shapes.

Dynamic and kinematic physics bodies automatically disturb horizontal water meshes when they
cross the surface or travel through it. Each contact sends a short, outward-moving wave packet;
its strength follows motion and its initial width follows the body's footprint. No script call
is needed. The visual effect displaces vertices and bends the lighting normal with the same
radial wave, so use a subdivided surface when the silhouette needs to move.

Impulses belong to one object and one original mesh primitive. Copies that share a mesh or
material, and other water primitives in that mesh, remain independent. The simulation keeps at
most 16 impulses for three seconds; drawing never advances their ages. Pausing simulation freezes
them, and recording uses the same simulation steps. They reset when the world changes. Temporal
motion uses the last snapshot actually drawn; a newly observed impulse starts with its current
age in both poses to avoid an invented first-frame velocity. These ripples are a visual response:
they do not apply buoyancy or forces to physics bodies and are not network-synchronized.

Contact detection uses the actual water triangles with a cached spatial tree. It supports rigid,
horizontal planar mesh primitives; skinned or tilted surfaces and Scatter copies do not generate
contacts. Body footprints use conservative world-aligned collider bounds, including spheres and
capsules. A small surface margin, emission cooldown and travel spacing suppress resting jitter.
Scripted position changes of dynamic bodies, characters and vehicles are treated as teleports;
scripted kinematic movement can create entry waves and wakes.

Work is bounded to the first 128 eligible water objects, 128 valid water primitives and
262,144 triangles per world, 256 moving bodies and 1,024 active body/surface pairs. Tilted or
oversized candidates still occupy a water-object slot. A primitive that exceeds the remaining
triangle budget is ignored as a whole. These bounds keep interaction work predictable for large scenes.

This first water material is for views above a lake or sea surface. Refraction samples only
opaque geometry visible on screen; transparent objects and other water layers are absent from
that snapshot. Screen-space reflections miss off-screen and hidden geometry and use the environment capture
when a ray misses. There is no planar reflection pass. Shore foam approximates the horizontal distance
to the intersection of the local water and visible-bottom tangent planes, without breaking-wave simulation.
Its world-space patches and softer pockets form an irregular band
rather than a uniform intersection line. Low-density pockets leave water uncovered; even dense
patches preserve some transmission instead of replacing the whole shallow surface with white.
Coverage fades in over a short contact distance and
fades out across the authored horizontal width; larger `foam_width` values broaden the band. The
pattern stays fixed in world space and does not drift with the render clock. Fine pores are filtered
by their projected footprint and converge to expected mean coverage when unresolved. Flat shallow
plateaus with no local shore intersection receive no foam. The local plane estimate uses the primary
opaque depth, not the refracted optical path. Occluded or off-screen bottom geometry, depth discontinuities,
and degenerate or almost parallel tangent planes produce no foam; they do not invent a hidden shore.
Curved terrain is only locally approximated, and rejected curvature can leave gaps. Nearly vertical
bottom walls are supported without dividing by the bottom normal's vertical component.

Traveling waves combine seven non-harmonic scales with distinct phases around one prevailing
direction. Slow spatial envelopes vary crest height; displacement and shading use the same
analytic gradient. Positive amplitude weights sum to one, and the envelopes never exceed one,
so `wave_height` remains the maximum displacement used by visibility bounds. Fragment normals
fade each traveling component when its phase becomes too fine for a pixel; discarded slope
variance adds bounded reflection roughness. Geometry and motion retain the full wave shape. This is a
procedural surface approximation, without wave interactions or a fluid spectrum simulation.
Refraction traces the visible depth field. When the refracted surface is hidden or outside the screen,
it keeps the undistorted opaque sample instead; this fallback cannot reveal geometry absent from the snapshot.
Depth discontinuities use a guarded, texel-matched color sample. When a ray misses, the visible
bottom's local tangent plane may estimate its absorption distance; this remains an approximation
for hidden or curved geometry.
Absorption filters the transmitted picture, but does not yet attenuate lighting on its way to submerged
objects; a lit bottom can therefore be brighter than in a full participating-medium render.
There is no underwater camera mode, buoyancy, fluid simulation, or wave collision. Use ordinary
scene meshes for water surfaces rather than Scatter copies.

The [optical comparison](water-validation.md) records a fixed-camera Cycles reference and
the remaining differences around refraction and incident lighting.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/command-line/

# The command line

For an MCP client, `redgem mcp <game> --read-only` exposes scene and API inspection over stdio.
See [MCP tools](mcp.md) for editing, headless runs, process events and permission options.

Besides opening the editor (`redgem my_game`), playing (`redgem my_game --play`), making a game
(`redgem new`) and building one (`redgem build`), `redgem` has tools that answer in a few lines
of text and end: they read and change a scene, play the game with no window, take a picture of
it, look it over, and say what the scripting API has. They are made for scripts, terminals and coding assistants: what they say
is short, and every problem they report says where it is and what to do instead.

Each one says more with `--help`. They end with exit code 0 when everything went well, 1 when
something is wrong with the game, and 2 when the command line was not understood.

## `redgem scene`: read and change a scene

A `scene.glb` is a binary file. `redgem scene` shows it as text, one line per object, and changes
it through the same code the editor saves with, so a scene changed here is saved exactly as the
editor would save it.

```console
$ redgem scene list games/platformer
scene main: 27 objects (#id name, then what differs from the defaults)
#0 Ground pos=0,-0.5,-4 scale=14,1,14 collider=box
#4 MovingPlatform pos=0,1.5,-25 scale=3,0.5,3 scripts=Mover axis=x body=kinematic distance=2.5 speed=1.2
#5 Player pos=0,1.1,0 scripts=Player body=character jump_speed=9 speed=6 tag=player
  #6 Visor pos=0,0.45,-0.35 scale=0.5,0.2,0.12
#7 Coin1 pos=0,1,-4 scripts=Coin tag=coin trigger=true
#24 Camera pos=0,6,9 rot=-28.6,0,0 camera scripts=CameraFollow distance=9 height=5 target=Player
#25 Sun pos=5,12,5 rot=-44.8,24.4,0 light=sun
...
```

A line says only what differs from an object's defaults: its position (`pos`, meters), rotation
(`rot`, degrees about X, Y and Z), scale when it is not 1, the mesh it shows when it is named
otherwise than the object, its light or camera, the classes of its scripts, and its custom
properties. Children are indented under their parent. `--depth 0` lists the top objects alone;
`--limit N` stops after N lines (200 unless said; `--limit 0` lists all).

**Naming an object.** `#12` is a persistent object identity, independent of its place in the
scene file. A path (`Player/Visor`) or a name works too when only one object has it; a name several
objects share is refused, with each of them listed by id and path. Identities survive saves,
renames and reparenting. New objects get hexadecimal identities: take them from `scene list` or
`scene add` and pass them back unchanged.

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `redgem scene list <game>` | every object, a line each |
| `redgem scene get <game> <object>` | everything about one object: its path, parent, placement, mesh and materials, light, camera, scripts, properties and children |
| `redgem scene set <game> <object> key=value...` | changes the object and saves the scene |
| `redgem scene add <game> <name> [--from <object>] [--parent <object>] [key=value...]` | adds an empty object, or a copy of another (with its children), and saves |
| `redgem scene remove <game> <object>` | removes the object and its children, and saves |
| `redgem scene diff <game> --against <before.glb>` | compares the current scene with an earlier save, without changing either file |

Every command takes `--scene <name>` for another scene than `scene.glb`: `--scene level2` is
`scenes/level2.glb`.

For `diff`, save a copy of the scene before editing, then pass that file to `--against`. Objects
are matched by their persistent identities: a rename or a reordered node array does not create
a new object. The summary counts added, removed and changed objects; details show the fields
that changed, including placement, hierarchy, properties, materials, image bytes, geometry,
cameras, lights, skin bindings and animation keys. Geometry and binary assets show content
fingerprints. Unused assets and glTF data the engine does not load are outside this comparison.
Re-encoding an image changes its fingerprint even if it looks identical.

`--limit N` bounds the detail lines (50 by default, `0` for all); the summary always counts every
object. Numeric object and material fields tolerate float differences up to 0.00001; custom
properties and fingerprinted asset values are compared exactly. Use an earlier save of the same
scene: independently exported scenes without persistent
identities cannot reliably identify the same objects.

What `set` (and `add`) take:

| Word | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `position=x,y,z` (or `pos=`) | where it is, in its parent's space |
| `rotation=x,y,z` (or `rot=`) | its rotation, in degrees |
| `scale=2` or `scale=1,2,1` | its size |
| `name=Gate` | a new name |
| `parent=Level` | moves it under another object, keeping where it is in the world; `parent=` moves it to the top |
| `prop.speed=2.5` | a custom property: `true`/`false`, a number, or a text (`prop.label="Big coin"`); `prop.speed=` removes it. A text that reads as a number is given in quotes that reach redgem: `prop.code='"12"'` (a list shows it as `code="12"`) |
| `script+=Door`, `script-=Door`, `script=Door,Sound` | attaches a behaviour, takes one off, or sets the list (`Door` is `scripts/door.rb`) |

```console
$ redgem scene set games/my_game Coin1 position=1,2,3 script+=Spinner
#7 Coin1 pos=1,2,3 scripts=Coin,Spinner tag=coin trigger=true
note: scripts/spinner.rb does not exist yet; it must define class Spinner
$ redgem scene add games/my_game Coin6 --from Coin5 position=3,3,-31
#27 Coin6 pos=3,3,-31 mesh=Coin5 scripts=Coin tag=coin trigger=true
```

A copy made with `--from` of a `prefab = true` template is an object of the scene, not another
template. Names are made unique as the editor makes them (`Wall`, then `Wall.001`), by `add` and
by `name=` alike; a name that starts with `#` or holds a `/` is refused, since it would read as an
id or a path.

The words of a `list` line are what `set` takes back: `pos=`, `rot=`, `scripts=Coin,Spin` (the
list of scripts), and a property as `speed=6` as well as `prop.speed=6`. A key that is a typo of
one of `set`'s (`positon=`) is refused rather than made a property; `prop.` makes any key a
property. `mesh=`, `light=` and `camera` say what an object is: they are taken back as they are,
and not changed.

## `redgem run`: play with no window

```console
$ redgem run games/my_game --seconds 3
error: scripts/coin.rb:12: Coin#update on 'Coin1' (behaviour disabled): undefined method 'spin' (NoMethodError)
ran main for 180 frames (3 s): 1 errors, 0 warnings
```

It plays the game with no window and no sound for a while (5 seconds unless `--seconds N` or
`--frames N` says otherwise), each frame one fixed step of 1/60 s with nothing pressed, so the same
run gives the same answer every time. It says each warning and error once (with how many times it
came), led by the place in the game's scripts it points at, then one line of summary, and ends
with an error when a script failed. `--scene level2` starts on another scene. What the game saves
goes to a folder of the run's own, deleted afterwards: a run never touches your progress.

## `redgem shot`: a picture of a moment

```console
$ redgem shot games/my_game shot.png --at 2
saved shot.png (512x288, scene main at 2 s)
```

It plays the game to that moment (1 second unless `--at` says otherwise; `--frames N` counts fixed
steps instead; at most an hour of the game, as for `run`) the way `run` does, draws
every frame off screen, and saves the picture of the one asked for. Small unless asked otherwise:
`--size 1280x720` for more. `--camera Name` shows the game through the camera of that object
instead of the scene's first camera; `--scene` starts on another scene. It needs a graphics card:
it opens a hidden window to draw with. The same moment gives the same picture.

## `redgem check`: look a game over

```console
$ redgem check games/my_game
error scripts/coin.rb:5: syntax error, unexpected end of file, expecting "'end'" (SyntaxError)
error scene main #20 Goal: scripts/goal_post.rb is not there; did you mean goal.rb?
error scripts/door.rb does not define class Door (attached in scene main #8 Door)
check: 3 errors, 0 warnings (12 scripts, 2 scenes)
```

Without playing the game it checks that every script compiles, every scene reads (with what the
loader warns of), every script a scene attaches is there and defines the class its name says, and
every `sky_image` is in `images/`. It lists a screenful of problems (`--all` lists every one).

`--run-tests` then runs the game's own tests (`tests/*_test.rb`, see
[Testing your game](testing.md)) with `redgem-test`, system tests with no window, and adds a line
per failure with the first error it said:

```console
$ redgem check games/my_game --run-tests
FAIL tests/score_test.rb: FAIL ScoreTest#test_a_coin_is_worth_ten: RedGemTest::Failure: expected 10, got 1
tests: 3 passed, 1 failed
check: 0 errors, 0 warnings (12 scripts, 2 scenes)
```

## `redgem api`: the scripting API

```console
$ redgem api Transform
Transform: Where an object is, how it is turned and how big it is.
  position                        its position in the world (Vector3)
  position = vector               moves it; a physics object is teleported
  rotate(degrees)                 turns it by those Euler degrees
  ...
```

`redgem api` alone lists the classes, a line each; `redgem api <Class>` the methods of one;
`redgem api --search <word>` the methods that have to do with a word (at most 20). `--json` says
the same as data, for tools. It is the [API reference](scripting/api.md), which `--markdown`
writes, and which is made from `docs/scripting/api.json`.

Errors that `run` and `shot` report come with a hint when they are common ones: a mistyped method
of one of the engine's classes gets the names near it, a class no script defines the file it is
looked for in, a scene the game lacks the scenes it has.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/assistants/

# Making games with an AI assistant

For an MCP client, [the stdio server](mcp.md) exposes the same developer commands through ten
tools (eleven with an editor), with a read-only mode, an allow list and cursor-based process
events. Register it once per game; `--editor auto` makes it use the open editor when there is one:

```sh
claude mcp add redgem -- redgem mcp /path/to/game --editor auto
```

A coding assistant that works in a terminal (one that reads files and runs commands) can make a
RedGem game with you: write behaviours, place objects in a level, play the game and read what went
wrong. RedGem gives it what it needs in text, so it does not have to guess an API it has never
seen, open a binary scene file or look at a window.

## What a new game comes with

`redgem new` (and the project hub) writes two files into every new game:

- **`AGENTS.md`**: the guide to the game, in the file most assistants look for: its layout, the
  commands below with examples, how to run its tests, its conventions (one behaviour per file,
  named after its class) and the 25 calls games make most, each with a line of Ruby. Under 120
  lines, so it costs little to read at the start of every session. The calls are taken from the
  same reference `redgem api` prints, so they are the engine's real ones.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**: one line that points at `AGENTS.md`, for the assistant that reads that file
  instead.

Edit `AGENTS.md` as the game grows: what an assistant should know about *your* game (its rules,
its scenes, what not to touch) belongs there.

## The commands it uses

Every one answers in a few lines and ends; each says more with `--help`. See
[The command line](command-line.md) for all of them.

| Need | Command |
|------|---------|
| What is in a level | `redgem scene list .` (a line per object: `#5 Player pos=0,1.1,0 scripts=Player tag=player`) |
| One object in full | `redgem scene get . Player` |
| Move, tune, attach | `redgem scene set . Coin1 position=1,2,3 prop.speed=2 script+=Spinner` |
| Add or remove | `redgem scene add . Coin6 --from Coin1 position=4,1,0`, `redgem scene remove . Coin6` |
| Is the game in order | `redgem check .` (and `--run-tests` to run its tests) |
| Does it play | `redgem run . --seconds 5`: each script error once, with its file and line |
| What it looks like | `redgem shot . shot.png --at 2`: a small picture of that moment |
| What a class can do | `redgem api`, `redgem api Transform`, `redgem api --search raycast` |

Scenes are changed through the same code the editor saves them with, so an edit made from the
command line is saved exactly as the editor would save it. Objects are named by a short id
(`#12`), a path or a name; a name several objects share is refused with each of them listed.

The common errors come with what to do about them: a mistyped method of one of the engine's
classes is answered with the names near it, a class no script defines with the file it is looked
for in, a scene the game lacks with the scenes it has.

```console
$ redgem run . --frames 30
error: scripts/goal.rb:3: Goal#start on 'Goal' (behaviour disabled): undefined method 'positon=' for Transform (NoMethodError) -> did you mean: position=, position (redgem api Transform)
ran main for 30 frames (0.5 s): 1 errors, 0 warnings
```

## A good loop

1. Ask for one thing at a time: "a coin that spins and adds to the score".
2. The assistant writes the behaviour in `scripts/`, attaches it with `redgem scene set`, then
   runs `redgem check .` and `redgem run .` and fixes what they report.
3. When it matters how it looks, `redgem shot` takes a picture to look at.
4. A system test in `tests/` (see [Testing your game](testing.md)) keeps it working:
   `redgem check . --run-tests`.
5. Open the editor (`redgem .`) to see and play it yourself.

## The same loop over MCP

| Need | Tool call |
|------|-----------|
| What is in a level | `scene_list` (50 lines unless `limit` says otherwise), then `scene_get` |
| Move, tune, attach, copy | `scene_edit` with `assignments`, and `from` to copy an object with its mesh |
| Does it play | `game_run`; `print` and `assert` read the game, e.g. `Scene.find('Coin6').transform.position` |
| Why does it fall through the floor | `game_query` `raycast` or `inspect` (velocity, grounded) |
| What it looks like | `game_shot` (512x288), or `editor` `capture` for the editor's view |
| What went wrong since last time | `events` with the last `cursor` |

A tool error says what to change (`frames: must be at most 600, not 601`), and a script that calls
`puts` is told to use `Debug.log`: scripts have no standard output.

## Keeping it cheap

What an assistant reads, it pays for. RedGem's answers are short on purpose; a few habits keep
them so:

- List a level with `--depth 0` or `--limit 20` first, then `get` the objects that matter.
- Ask `redgem api <Class>` or `redgem api --search <word>` instead of reading the whole reference.
- Prefer `redgem run` (text) to `redgem shot` (a picture) to find out whether something works; a
  picture is for how it looks. Shots are 512x288 unless asked otherwise.
- `redgem check` lists a screenful of problems; fix those before asking for `--all`.

## The manual for assistants

The manual's site has `llms.txt`, an index of its pages with a line about each, and
`llms-full.txt`, every page in one file to search. The docs build writes both
(`tools/docs/llms_txt.py`). The API reference is also data: `redgem api --json`, and
`docs/scripting/api.json` in the repository, which tests keep in step with the engine.

## Repeating a headless session

`redgem run` uses fixed steps of 1/60 s and a random seed of 0. Use `--seed N` to repeat another
Ruby and particle random stream, including random values read while scripts first load. A seed
is a whole number from 0 to 2147483647. Scatter requests keep their own explicit seeds. Network
traffic, web responses and scripts that read external clocks or files are outside this replay.

Keyboard input comes from a JSON file. Each event replaces the whole set of held keys before
its zero-based frame; keys remain held until the next event. An empty list releases them:

```json
[
  {"frame": 0, "keys": ["w"]},
  {"frame": 30, "keys": ["w", "space"]},
  {"frame": 31, "keys": ["w"]},
  {"frame": 120, "keys": []}
]
```

```sh
redgem run my-game --seed 42 --frames 180 --input input.json \
  --assert "Scene.find('Player').transform.position.y > -10" \
  --print "Scene.find('Player').transform.position" --every 60
```

`--assert` evaluates a Ruby expression after every frame and fails the run at its first false or
nil result. `--until` stops successfully when its expression becomes true; reaching the frame
limit or quitting without satisfying it fails. Both expressions use ordinary Ruby truthiness
(0 is true). `--print` evaluates an expression every `--every` frames (60 by default) and on the
last frame, showing its Ruby `inspect` value with a one-based frame number. Values and total
output are capped; increase `--every` to keep a longer run concise.

Expressions run in the game's interpreter with its script timeout, and can call game APIs.
Use them to read state: a mutation or a call to `rand` changes the session too. The order is
input, game frame, assertion, periodic print, stop condition. On an early stop, a final print
runs after the stop condition. A syntax error, exception or timeout in any expression fails the
run with its frame and option. The command exits 0 on success, 1 for a failed run, and 2 for
invalid options or an invalid input file. Input currently covers keyboard state only.

## Object identities

An object's `#id` identifies that object across saves, renames and changes to its parent. Removing
another object does not renumber it. Objects made, duplicated, pasted or imported in the editor
get new identities; undo and redo restore the same identities with the objects.

A scene that has never been saved by the editor starts with numeric identities (`#0`, `#1`, and
so on). Its next save persists them in the scene. New objects use compact hexadecimal identities.
Always take an identity from `redgem scene list` or the result of `scene add`, and pass it back
unchanged; it is not an array index. Names and hierarchy paths remain valid selectors too.

The file keeps identities in the private `REDGEM_object_id` glTF extension, with an `id` string
on each node. It is listed in `extensionsUsed` so other glTF tools can ignore it. The engine
repairs invalid or duplicate identities with a warning. An external exporter that drops this
extension creates a scene without those persistent identities; list its objects again before
editing it. Identical names in different scenes do not identify the same object.

Before editing a scene, keep a copy of its `.glb`. Afterwards, use
`redgem scene diff . --against /path/to/before.glb` to inspect the changes by persistent identity.
It reports object additions, removals and changed fields without writing either file. `--scene`
chooses another scene and `--limit` caps the details; see [the command line](command-line.md).

## The Agent panel

The editor has a chat with a coding agent: the **Agent** tab beside the Inspector (View > Agent
shows or hides it). You talk to the agent there as you would in its own terminal chat. It works in
the game's folder, and it gets the editor's MCP tools ([MCP tools](mcp.md#live-editor)), so it can
list, select, move, add and remove objects in the open scene, play and stop the game, read the
editor's events and errors, and look at the viewport.

The editor speaks the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) (ACP) to agents. Each
agent is its own program, an open-source adapter that the editor starts:

| Agent | Adapter | Install |
|-------|---------|---------|
| Claude Code | `claude-agent-acp` | `npm i -g @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp` |
| Codex | `codex-acp` | `npm i -g @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` |

Both need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org). If the adapter is not installed but `npx` is, the editor
runs it with `npx --yes <package>`, which downloads it the first time. If neither is there, the
panel says what to install.

The adapters log in the way their own command line tools do, and the editor never asks for a
password. Log in once in a terminal (`claude`, then `/login`; or `codex login`, or an
`OPENAI_API_KEY`), then start a new session in the panel. If an agent asks for a login, the panel
shows its message and how to log in.

### Using it

1. Pick an agent at the top of the panel. Your first message starts a session (the **+** button
   starts a new one).
2. Write in the box at the bottom. **Enter** sends, **Shift+Enter** starts a new line.
3. The answer streams in as markdown. Code blocks have a **Copy** button. Thinking is folded under
   *Thinking*, and each tool call is a card with its status; open it to see its input, its output
   and file changes as `-`/`+` lines. The agent's plan shows as a checklist.
4. Before the agent acts, it may ask: the question shows its options (allow once, allow always,
   reject). **Stop** ends the turn and answers any open question "cancelled".
5. The paperclip attaches the selected objects to your next message, as `redgem scene get`
   describes them, so you can ask about "these" without naming them.

The agent reads and writes files through the editor only inside the game's folder. Paths that
leave it are refused, and so are paths through symbolic links. Its first session turns on the
editor's local bridge ([MCP tools](mcp.md#live-editor)) and hands the agent
`redgem mcp <game> --editor <connection>` as its MCP server. Its edits to the scene are undo steps
like yours, and they stay unsaved until you or the agent save.

### Past conversations

A conversation is not lost when the editor closes. The editor remembers each game's last 20
conversations: which agent each was had with, its first message as a title, and when it was last
used. When the editor opens the game again, the last conversation comes back as it was left. The
clock button beside **+** lists the others, and picking one reopens it with its agent.

The agent keeps the conversation itself. Reopening one asks the agent to replay it (ACP's
`session/load`, which both Claude Code's and Codex's adapters support), and the transcript is
rebuilt from that replay. An agent that cannot replay conversations starts a new one, and the panel
says so; the list stays. The list is kept in `agent-sessions.json` in your RedGem settings folder,
not in the game's folder, so it is not shared with the game.

### Your own agents

The gear button opens the list of agents. Each one has a name, a command, arguments (one per line)
and environment variables (`NAME=value`). Any program that speaks ACP over its standard streams can
be added. The list is kept in `agents.json` in your RedGem settings folder (`~/.config/redgem/` on
Linux). Variables are stored there as plain text, so an API key there can be read by anyone who can
read that file. **Restore** brings back the Claude Code and Codex presets.

---

Page: https://carlosdanielpohlod.github.io/redgem-site/manual/mcp/

# MCP tools

Start a local MCP server for one game:

```sh
redgem mcp /path/to/game --read-only
```

Configure your MCP client to launch the `redgem` executable with those arguments. It reads
newline-delimited JSON-RPC from standard input and writes only protocol responses to standard
output. Native library output goes to standard error. Closing input stops the server.
By default it opens no listening socket and works on files. Add `--editor` to connect to an
editor that explicitly enabled its local bridge (see below).

The server supports the MCP `2026-07-28` per-request metadata protocol and the `2025-11-25`,
`2025-06-18` and `2025-03-26` initialization handshakes (a client asking for one of them gets it). Modern clients can discover capabilities with `server/discover` and
must supply their protocol version and client capabilities in each request's `params._meta`.
Legacy clients send `initialize`, then `notifications/initialized`, before using tools.

## Tools and permissions

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `scene_list` | Lists objects, taking optional `scene`, `limit` (default 50, `0` for all) and `depth`. |
| `scene_get` | Reads one `object` by persistent `#id`, unique name or hierarchy path. |
| `scene_edit` | Takes `action` (`set`, `add`, `remove`), `object` and optional `assignments` (`key=value` strings), `from`, `parent`, `scene`. Removal requires `confirm: true`. Saves the scene file. |
| `scene_diff` | Compares with an earlier scene file named by `against`, inside the game. |
| `game_run` | Plays headlessly with `frames` (default 60, maximum 600), `seed`, `input`, `assert`, `until`, `print`, `every`, `scene`. |
| `game_check` | Checks scripts, scenes and assets; does not run the game's test files. |
| `game_shot` | Returns a PNG picture of the saved game at `at` seconds (default 1), `width` pixels wide (default 512, 16:9), optionally through another `camera`. |
| `game_query` | Asks the playing game: `inspect` an `object`, `raycast` `from` one point `to` another, or `overlap` a sphere `at` a point with a `radius`. |
| `api` | Reads the API index, a `class`, or a `search`. |
| `events` | Reads this server's log history with `since`, `limit` (default 20, maximum 32), `level`. |

`game_run` expressions run in the game after each frame and can use anything scripts can, for
example `print: "Scene.find('Player').transform.position"` or
`assert: "Physics.raycast(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), Vector3.down)"`.

`game_query` answers in short lines with rounded numbers. `inspect` gives the object's world
position and rotation, its body, velocity and whether a character is grounded, and only those
props that scripts changed since the scene loaded. Points are `x,y,z` strings in meters. Without
an editor in Play, it plays the saved game for `frames` (default 60) first, as `game_run` does:

```json
{"action": "inspect", "object": "Player"}
{"action": "raycast", "from": "0,5,0", "to": "0,-5,0"}
{"action": "overlap", "at": "4,1,-3", "radius": 1.5}
```

```text
after 60 frames: #5 Player pos=0,0.8,0 body=character vel=0,-0.33,0 grounded
after 60 frames: 2 hits, nearest first:
#5 Player at 0,1.62,0 normal=0,1,0 dist=3.38
#0 Ground at 0,0,0 normal=0,1,0 dist=5
```

`game_shot` draws in a separate `redgem shot` process with a hidden window. A graphics driver
that crashes takes only that process down, and the call reports it. It needs a display. Without one (no `DISPLAY` on Linux)
it returns a tool error that says so, and the server keeps answering. Some MCP clients start
servers with only a few environment variables; pass `DISPLAY` in the server's configuration
if pictures are wanted. Prefer `game_run` to find out whether something works and use pictures
for how it looks.

Invalid arguments come back as tool errors (`isError: true`) naming the argument and what it
accepts, such as `frames: must be at most 600, not 601`, so the model can correct the call.
Unknown or disabled tools remain JSON-RPC errors.

`--read-only` exposes only `scene_list`, `scene_get`, `scene_diff`, `api` and `events`; the
`game_*` tools execute the game's scripts and are disabled. It also
rejects calls to disabled tools, even if the client remembers an earlier tool list. For a smaller
surface, add an exact comma-separated allow list:

```sh
redgem mcp /path/to/game --read-only --allow scene_list,scene_get,api,events
```

Without `--read-only`, the tools can save edits and execute the configured game's Ruby scripts.
Run only games you trust. A run expression can mutate state or use networking; read-only mode
disables execution entirely. The configured game directory stays fixed for the life of the
process. Input replay and comparison files must be regular files inside it, without symbolic
links. These restrictions protect tooling paths; they do not sandbox native game code.

Without `--editor`, edits go through the file-based scene commands. Close the editor while
editing its files this way. Keep an earlier save and inspect `scene_diff` after an edit.
`from` is available only in file mode; `parent` also works when adding a live empty object.
With `--editor auto`, check `editor` `status` to know whether calls reach an editor.

## Live editor

Start the editor with its bridge explicitly enabled:

```sh
redgem /path/to/game --editor-bridge
```

The terminal prints the path of a private `connection.json` in the user's RedGem data folder.
Let the MCP server find it on every call, so one client configuration survives editor restarts:

```sh
redgem mcp /path/to/game --editor auto
```

With `auto`, each call uses the newest running editor of that game. When none answers, the
scene tools, `game_query` and `events` work on the saved files and this server instead, and
their answer starts with `(no editor is running: answered from the saved files)`; the `editor`
tool returns an error saying how to start an editor with its bridge. A connection file whose
port refuses connections belongs to an editor that is gone and is deleted. A listener that does
not prove itself (below) is skipped for a minute, so it delays at most one call a minute by about
a second. To pin one editor instance, pass its file:

```sh
redgem mcp /path/to/game --editor /path/to/connection.json
```

If that editor exits, calls fail with an error that says how to restart it. A pinned editor
always answers scene edits live, so its `scene_edit` schema leaves out `from`.

With `auto`, an `events` cursor belongs to whichever process answered: the editor, or this server
when no editor is open. After an editor opens or closes, start again from `since: 0`.

Scene listing, object details and scene comparison now read the editor's unsaved document.
